title: Forecasting US Industrial Production
text:
Key findings

The series needs transforming before modelling. Industrial production has a trend, a strong seasonal pattern and two large shocks (2008–2009 and 2020). Unit root tests (KPSS, ADF, Phillips-Perron) agree that it is non-stationary; the HEGY test shows a stochastic trend (p = 0.43) but a deterministic seasonal pattern (seasonal unit roots rejected, p < 0.01).
No model clearly wins. With a single forecast origin (June 2016), SARIMA looked best (RMSE 2.93). A rolling-origin evaluation, which re-estimates the models every month, is more reliable: SARIMA, ETS and Holt-Winters are statistically tied one month ahead (RMSE 1.96–2.07) and all significantly beat a seasonal naive benchmark (4.11). From about 4 months ahead the seasonal naive forecast has a lower RMSE, but the difference is not statistically significant at any horizon (Diebold-Mariano p ≥ 0.29).
Consumer sentiment has statistically significant but small predictive content. The two series are not cointegrated. In a VAR with seasonal dummies, sentiment Granger-causes industrial production (p = 0.003) but not the reverse (p = 0.42), and it explains about 5% of production’s forecast variance. A typical sentiment shock (about 4 points) raises the production index by about 0.4–0.5 points over a year. Adding sentiment to the model does not improve out-of-sample forecasts: neither the Diebold-Mariano test nor the Clark-West test for nested models finds a gain (Clark-West one-sided p between 0.19 and 0.87).
Outlook: a SARIMA model re-estimated on all data forecasts the index at around 100–102 through April 2028 (95% interval 84–120).

title: Forecasting US Industrial Production
text:
Limitations

Prediction intervals are probably too narrow in crises. Model residuals show ARCH effects (volatility clustering) and heavy tails, while the intervals assume constant, normal errors.
The pandemic dominates the errors. A few months in 2020 produce the largest forecast errors; results excluding them are reported as a robustness check, and the main conclusions do not change.
Revised data, not real-time data. The backtest uses the data as revised by December 2025, not the figures available to a forecaster at each date.
One series and one sample. The conclusions apply to this index and this period.
Seasonal differencing is a modelling choice. The HEGY test points to deterministic seasonality; a model with a first difference and monthly dummies was not tested as a forecasting alternative to SARIMA.

title: Forecasting US Industrial Production
text:
How the analysis is organised

Univariate models: visual analysis, stationarity and seasonality tests, ARMA, SARIMA, ETS, Holt-Winters, a seasonal naive benchmark, residual diagnostics, single-origin and rolling-origin evaluation, and the forecast to 2028.
VAR analysis: consumer sentiment, Johansen cointegration test, VAR with seasonal dummies, Granger causality, impulse responses, variance decomposition, an out-of-sample test of the value of sentiment (Diebold-Mariano and Clark-West) and a 24-month forecast.

Univariate models
text:
Visual analysis


Code
autoplot(ip_ts) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)")








Figure 1: US industrial production, total index





The series has a strong upward trend between 1990 and 2008, so its mean is not constant, which is a first sign of non-stationarity. Two major shocks stand out: the collapse during the 2008–2009 financial crisis and the very sharp but short-lived drop during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The trend and the level shifts call for formal unit root testing.


Code
ggtsdisplay(ip_ts)








Figure 2: Series, ACF and PACF in levels





The ACF decays very slowly and almost linearly, staying far above the significance bands: the classic pattern of a non-stationary (unit root) process. The PACF has a large spike at lag 1 and significant spikes at the seasonal lags 12 and 24. Visually, the series needs both a regular difference (for the trend) and a seasonal difference at lag 12.


Code
ggsubseriesplot(ip_ts) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Index (2017 = 100)")








Figure 3: Seasonal subseries: one panel per month, blue line = monthly mean





The monthly means differ: June and August have the highest average production, while April and July are lower. Unequal monthly means are visual evidence of a seasonal component, which motivates the HEGY test for seasonal unit roots.

The HEGY test checks for unit roots at the zero frequency (t_1, an ordinary stochastic trend) and at each seasonal frequency (t_2 and the F-statistics). Because the series has a trend and a seasonal pattern, the test regression includes a constant, a trend and monthly dummies.

For t_1, p = 0.4269 (> 0.05): the zero-frequency unit root is not rejected, so the series needs a regular (first) difference.
At all seasonal frequencies the p-values are below 0.01: seasonal unit roots are rejected. The seasonal pattern is deterministic (a stable pattern by month), not stochastic.

Strictly, this points to a first difference with monthly dummies rather than a seasonal difference. The analysis below follows the usual SARIMA route with both a log transformation and a seasonal difference at lag 12, which is also what auto.arima() selects. Seasonally differencing a series without seasonal unit roots can over-difference it; this would show up as a seasonal MA coefficient close to −1 in the SARIMA model, which is checked below.

title: Univariate models
text:
Train / test split


Code
n_total <- length(ip_ts)
n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_total)

ip_train <- window(ip_ts, end = time(ip_ts)[n_train])
ip_test <- window(ip_ts, start = time(ip_ts)[n_train + 1])
ip_train_log <- window(ip_log, end = time(ip_log)[n_train])

h <- length(ip_test)


The first 75% of the sample (318 months, to Jun 2016) is used to estimate the models; the last 106 months (Jul 2016 to Apr 2025) are kept for out-of-sample evaluation. The forecast horizon h equals the length of the test set, so RMSE, MAE and MAPE can be computed on it.

SARIMA forecast


Code
# Back-transform to index levels. The same model (same coefficients) is applied
# to the series with lambda = 0, i.e. a log transformation, so forecast()
# returns exp() of the log forecasts: the point forecast is the median of the
# forecast distribution and the interval bounds (quantiles) carry over exactly.
sarima_lvl <- Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0)
sarima_real <- forecast(sarima_lvl, h = h)

# For comparison: the bias-adjusted mean forecast
sarima_mean <- forecast(Arima(ip_train, model = sarima_final, lambda = 0, biasadj = TRUE), h = h)
sarima_mean_rmse <- accuracy(sarima_mean$mean, ip_test)[1, "RMSE"]

autoplot(sarima_real) +
  autolayer(ip_test, series = "Test data") +
  labs(title = NULL, x = "Year", y = "Index (2017 = 100)", colour = NULL)








Figure 8: SARIMA forecast (back-transformed to index levels) against the test data






The forecasts are made for the log of the index and converted back with exp(). This gives the median forecast, and the prediction intervals stay valid because quantiles are preserved by exp(). The mean forecast would be higher by roughly half the forecast variance, which grows quickly with the horizon: the gap is 0.1 index points after 12 months but 8.3 after 106 months, and the RMSE on the test period would be 4.63 instead of 2.93. The median is used as the point forecast.
The forecast (blue) follows the centre of the test data (2016–2025) closely from this single origin; the rolling-origin evaluation below gives a more complete picture of out-of-sample performance.
The 2020 COVID-19 shock appears as a large exogenous deviation; the data later return to the forecast path.
The uncertainty fan widens asymmetrically, as expected for long-horizon forecasts on a log scale.

Rolling-origin evaluation
Here the models are re-estimated every month of the test period on all data available up to that month (an expanding window) and forecast the next 1 to 12 months, as an analyst updating the forecast every month would do. Each model keeps the specification selected on the training data; only its parameters are re-estimated. SARIMA forecasts are medians, as above.


Code
max_h <- 12
sarima_order <- arimaorder(sarima_final)

# Forecast functions with the specifications chosen on the training data
ets_spec <- ets_auto$components  # error, trend, season, damped
forecast_functions <- list(
  SARIMA = function(x, h) {
    forecast(Arima(x, order = sarima_order[c("p", "d", "q")],
                   seasonal = sarima_order[c("P", "D", "Q")], lambda = 0), h = h)
  },
  ETS = function(x, h) {
    forecast(ets(x, model = paste0(ets_spec[1], ets_spec[2], ets_spec[3]),
                 damped = as.logical(ets_spec[4])), h = h)
  },
  `Holt-Winters` = function(x, h) hw(x, seasonal = "additive", h = h),
  `Seasonal naive` = function(x, h) snaive(x, h = h)
)

# Row t, column k = error of the k-step forecast made with data up to month t.
# The first origin is the end of the training sample (June 2016).
cv_errors <- lapply(forecast_functions, function(f) {
  tsCV(ip_ts, f, h = max_h, initial = n_train - 1)
})

# Actual value and target date of each k-step forecast, aligned with cv_errors

target_value <- function(k) c(as.numeric(ip_ts)[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k))
target_time <- function(k) c(as.numeric(time(ip_ts))[-(1:k)], rep(NA, k))

cv_accuracy <- function(k, exclude_covid = FALSE) {
  keep <- !is.na(target_value(k))
  if (exclude_covid) {
    keep <- keep & !(target_time(k) >= 2020 + 2 / 12 & target_time(k) < 2021.5)
  }
  t(sapply(cv_errors, function(E) {
    e <- E[, k]
    ok <- keep & !is.na(e)
    c(Forecasts = sum(ok),
      RMSE = sqrt(mean(e[ok]^2)),
      MAE = mean(abs(e[ok])),
      `MAPE (%)` = 100 * mean(abs(e[ok] / target_value(k)[ok])))
  }))
}

Diebold-Mariano tests
The Diebold-Mariano test compares the squared errors of SARIMA with those of each other model on the same forecast origins. The null hypothesis is equal accuracy; a negative statistic means SARIMA has smaller errors. For 12-month forecasts, consecutive errors overlap, and h = 12 makes the test account for the resulting autocorrelation.


Code

for (k in c(1, max_h)) {
  for (m in setdiff(names(cv_errors), "SARIMA")) {
    a <- cv_errors$SARIMA[, k]
    b <- cv_errors[[m]][, k]
    ok <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)
    test <- dm.test(a[ok], b[ok], alternative = "two.sided", h = k, power = 2)
    dm_rows[[length(dm_rows) + 1]] <- data.frame(
      Horizon = paste(k, if (k == 1) "month" else "months"),
      Comparison = paste("SARIMA vs", m),
      `DM statistic` = round(unname(test$statistic), 3),
      `p-value` = signif(test$p.value, 3),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }
}

Over the 20 months shown, the band excludes zero only 1 and 10 months after the shock, so the effect is concentrated in the first month and is short-lived.
For a shock to industrial production, the band excludes zero only 12 months after the shock: production shocks have essentially no effect on consumer confidence.

With 90% bands, about 2 of 20 horizons are expected to exclude zero by chance alone, so isolated significant points far from the shock should not be over-interpreted.

section: Does sentiment improve forecasts out of sample?
text:
Does sentiment improve forecasts out of sample?
The Granger test uses the whole sample. A stricter, practical question is whether sentiment improves real forecasts. The VAR is compared with:

an AR(12) model for the change in industrial production with the same constant and monthly dummies, i.e. the VAR equation for IPB_d without the lags of sentiment. The only difference between the two models is the information in consumer sentiment;
the SARIMA model from the univariate analysis, ARIMA(3,1,0)(0,1,1)[12] on log data.

As in the univariate rolling-origin evaluation, every month from June 2016 to March 2025 the three models are re-estimated on the data available up to that month and forecast industrial production 1 to 12 months ahead. Forecasts of monthly changes are added up to give index levels.


Code
n_obs <- length(ip_ts)
n_train <- floor(0.75 * n_obs)  # same split as the univariate analysis (June 2016)
max_h <- 12

ip_values <- as.numeric(ip_ts)
ip_diff <- ts(diff(ip_values), start = c(1990, 2), frequency = 12)
umc_diff <- diff(as.numeric(umc_ts))

oos_errors <- list(
  VAR = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h),
  `AR(12), no sentiment` = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h),
  SARIMA = matrix(NA, n_obs, max_h)
)

for (t in n_train:(n_obs - 1)) {
  m <- t - 1                        # differences available at origin t
  steps <- 1:min(max_h, n_obs - t)  # horizons with an observed outcome
  actual <- ip_values[t + steps]

  # VAR with sentiment
  v <- VAR(data.frame(IPB_d = ip_diff[1:m], UMCSENT_d = umc_diff[1:m]),
           p = var_p, type = "const", season = 12)
  fc_var <- predict(v, n.ahead = max_h)$fcst$IPB_d[, "fcst"]

  # Same equation without sentiment; CSS gives least-squares estimates like the VAR
  x <- window(ip_diff, end = time(ip_diff)[m])
  ar <- Arima(x, order = c(var_p, 0, 0), xreg = seasonaldummy(x), method = "CSS")
  fc_ar <- forecast(ar, h = max_h, xreg = seasonaldummy(x, h = max_h))$mean

  # SARIMA on log data (median forecast)
  s <- Arima(ts(ip_values[1:t], start = c(1990, 1), frequency = 12),
             order = c(3, 1, 0), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1), lambda = 0)
  fc_sarima <- forecast(s, h = max_h)$mean

  oos_errors$VAR[t, steps] <- actual - (ip_values[t] + cumsum(fc_var))[steps]
  oos_errors$`AR(12), no sentiment`[t, steps] <- actual - (ip_values[t] + cumsum(as.numeric(fc_ar)))[steps]
  oos_errors$SARIMA[t, steps] <- actual - as.numeric(fc_sarima)[steps]
}

Clark-West test for nested models
The VAR and the AR(12) model are nested: the AR model is the VAR equation with the sentiment coefficients set to zero. If sentiment has no predictive value, both models estimate the same thing, but the VAR also estimates 12 coefficients whose true value is zero; this estimation noise makes its forecasts slightly worse even when sentiment is useful. The Diebold-Mariano test compares raw squared errors, so for nested models it is biased towards the smaller model and rarely rejects equal accuracy.
The Clark-West (2007) test corrects the squared errors of the larger model for this noise, by adding back the squared difference between the two forecasts. It is one-sided: the alternative hypothesis is that the VAR forecasts better than the AR model. For 12-month forecasts the standard error accounts for the overlap between consecutive forecasts (Newey-West with 11 lags).


Code
clark_west <- function(e_small, e_large, h) {
  ok <- !is.na(e_small) & !is.na(e_large)
  es <- e_small[ok]
  el <- e_large[ok]
  # Forecast difference: y_hat_small - y_hat_large = e_large - e_small
  adjusted <- es^2 - (el^2 - (es - el)^2)
  fit <- lm(adjusted ~ 1)
  se <- if (h == 1) {
    sqrt(vcov(fit)[1, 1])
  } else {
    sqrt(sandwich::NeweyWest(fit, lag = h - 1, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = TRUE)[1, 1])
  }
  stat <- unname(coef(fit)[1] / se)
  data.frame(
    Horizon = paste(h, if (h == 1) "month" else "months"),
    Forecasts = sum(ok),
    `CW statistic` = round(stat, 3),
    `p-value (one-sided)` = round(1 - pnorm(stat), 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

Sentiment is a statistically significant predictor in sample (Granger test), but this does not translate into better out-of-sample forecasts. A likely reason is that estimating 12 extra sentiment coefficients adds noise that offsets the small amount of information they carry. This is a common result in macroeconomic forecasting: in-sample significance is a weak guide to forecasting value.
